question: As a nurse, why is your role in medication administration so important?

options.A: Prescribing the correct dosage based on lab results
options.B: Manufacturing safe chemical compounds for hospital use
options.C: Acting as the final safety barrier before the drug reaches the patient
options.D: Selling pharmaceutical supplies to hospital wards

explanation: You are the last line of defense! By double-checking the order and the patient right before giving the drug, you catch mistakes that might have slipped through earlier. Great job keeping patients safe! [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h1)

question: You look at a medication order and the dose looks unsafe. What should you do?

options.A: Withhold the drug and contact the prescriber to clarify the order
options.B: Administer the medication anyway since the doctor holds the liability
options.C: Change the dose independently based on personal experience
options.D: Ask another patient to take the extra dose to avoid waste

explanation: Never guess or blindly follow a suspicious order! You have a legal duty to protect your patient, so always pause, hold the drug, and check with the doctor first. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h1)

question: Before giving any medication, how many unique patient identifiers must you check?

options.A: No identifiers are needed if the nurse knows the patient well

explanation: Always use at least two ways to identify your patient (like their name and hospital number) before handing over meds. It's a simple habit that stops mix-ups! [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h2)

question: You are about to give an oral pill, but the chart says the drug should be given intravenously (IV). What do you do?

options.A: Crush the tablet and mix it with sterile water for an injection
options.B: Stop and clarify the route with the prescriber because giving drugs by the wrong route is dangerous
options.C: Give the pill by mouth anyway since the active ingredient is the same
options.D: Skip the dose completely and document that the patient refused

explanation: Route matters immensely! Changing how a drug enters the body can cause serious harm. Always pause and clarify the order if things don't match up. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h2)

question: Why do nurses check vital signs before giving certain medications?

options.A: To fulfill a mandatory paperwork requirement for hospital insurance
options.B: To make sure the patient's current physical status is safe for that specific drug
options.C: To distract the patient from feeling nervous about the injection
options.D: To test if the thermometer and blood pressure cuff are working correctly

explanation: Checking vitals first helps you catch things like low blood pressure or a slow heart rate before giving a drug that could drop them even lower. Safety first! [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h3)

question: What critical allergy information must you check before giving any new drug?

options.B: Known drug allergies and past adverse reactions
options.C: Family history of seasonal pollen allergies

explanation: Always ask about past drug reactions! It's a quick question that protects your patient from severe allergic responses like anaphylaxis. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h3)

question: On a busy hospital ward, what is the most common reason medication preparation errors happen?

options.A: Patients refusing to take bitter-tasting liquids
options.B: Pharmacies sending drugs in alphabetical order
options.C: Lack of basic mathematical formulas in textbooks
options.D: Distractions and interruptions during the setup process

explanation: Interruptions break your concentration easily. That's why creating a quiet zone for yourself during drug prep is such a great nursing habit! [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h4)

question: What should you do if you are unsure about a drug dosage calculation?

options.A: Give half the amount to be safe and wait for complaints
options.B: Have a second nurse independently calculate and verify the dose
options.C: Call the hospital security team to supervise the injection
options.D: Guess the amount based on the patient's physical size

explanation: Two brains are better than one! Getting an independent double-check from a colleague is a gold standard for catching math errors before they reach the patient. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h4)

question: Why shouldn't you crush enteric-coated oral tablets?

options.A: Crushing destroys the protective coating, which can irritate the stomach or ruin the drug's timed release
options.B: It changes the pill color, which confuses the pharmacy department
options.C: It makes the pill powder too sweet for the patient to swallow comfortably
options.D: The crushed powder will instantly clog standard drinking straws

explanation: That special coating is there for a reason! It protects the stomach lining and controls how fast the drug dissolves. Crushing ruins that design. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h5)

question: What is the correct way to apply a new transdermal medication patch?

options.A: Remove the old patch and clean the skin before placing the new one on a different site
options.B: Use bare fingers to rub the sticky side firmly onto hairy skin areas
options.C: Cut the patch in half if the prescribed dose is too strong for the patient
options.D: Put the new patch directly on top of the old one to keep the medication level high

explanation: Always take off the old patch first and pick a fresh skin site! Rotating spots prevents skin irritation, and removing the old one prevents accidental overdoses. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h5)

question: Why must you document a medication immediately after giving it, rather than waiting until the end of your shift?

options.A: Because hospital computers automatically shut down at noon
options.B: To finish paperwork quickly so the nurse can take a break
options.C: To prevent another nurse from accidentally giving a second duplicate dose
options.D: To let the pharmacy know the pill bottle is now empty

explanation: Immediate charting lets the whole healthcare team know the job is done, keeping the patient safe from getting a accidental double dose later! [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h6)

question: After giving a patient a strong painkiller through an IV, what is your most important follow-up duty?

options.A: Check back within a short window to evaluate pain relief and watch for breathing problems
options.B: Discharge the patient immediately since pain management is complete
options.C: Document that the patient is cured of all chronic illnesses
options.D: Wait until the next morning to ask if the pain went away

explanation: Powerful painkillers need close monitoring. You want to make sure the pain is actually easing up, and that the patient's breathing stays safe and steady. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h6)

question: What is the very first thing you should do if you realize a medication error has happened?

options.A: Write an angry message in the chat group for the next shift
options.B: Call the hospital lawyer to prepare legal defense documents
options.C: Hide the empty medication wrapper in a pocket to destroy evidence
options.D: Assess the patient's clinical condition and provide any needed emergency care

explanation: The patient always comes first! Checking on their physical condition and providing any necessary care takes priority over paperwork and reporting. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h7)

question: What is the main goal of filing an incident report after a medication mistake?

options.A: To collect financial fines from the pharmacy department
options.B: To provide gossip material for the nursing station
options.C: To identify system flaws and prevent future mistakes
options.D: To ensure the responsible nurse gets fired immediately

explanation: Incident reports aren't about blame—they help the team figure out what went wrong in the workflow so we can fix it and protect future patients. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h7)

question: Which ethical principle gives a competent patient the right to refuse a prescribed medication?
explanation: Autonomy is all about respecting the patient's right to make independent choices about their own body and healthcare journey. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h8)

question: Which of these statements is FALSE regarding legal accountability in drug administration?

options.A: A nurse is completely free from liability if a doctor wrote the incorrect order
options.B: A nurse can lose their nursing license for gross negligence in medication handling
options.C: A nurse is legally responsible for verifying every drug before giving it
options.D: A nurse must follow facility policies and state scope of practice laws

explanation: You can't just blame the doctor! Nurses share legal accountability and cannot blindly give a harmful drug just because it was prescribed. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h8)
